cards.front: What year did the French Revolution begin?
cards.back: 1789 - The storming of the Bastille on July 14th marked the symbolic start.

cards.back: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789)

questions.question: Which organelle is known as the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria produce ATP through cellular respiration, providing energy for cell functions.

questions.question: What protects and supports a plant cell that animal cells lack?
questions.explanation: The cell wall provides structural support and protection. It's made of cellulose in plants.

questions.question: Where is DNA primarily located in a eukaryotic cell?
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains most of the cell's genetic material (DNA), though mitochondria have their own DNA too.

questions.question: Which organelle synthesizes proteins?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes read mRNA and assemble amino acids into proteins. They're found free in cytoplasm or on rough ER.

questions.question: What is the function of the Golgi apparatus?
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids for transport or secretion.

lesson.title: Newton's Laws of Motion

sections.title: First Law: Inertia
sections.content: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion... unless something messes with it. That 'something' is an unbalanced force. This is why your coffee spills when the bus brakes suddenly - the coffee wanted to keep moving forward, but your cup (and the bus) stopped.
sections.keyTakeaway: Objects resist changes to their motion. No force = no change.

sections.title: Second Law: F = ma
sections.content: Force equals mass times acceleration. The heavier something is, the more force you need to move it. That's why pushing a shopping cart is easy, but pushing a car is... not. This law is literally the foundation of rocket science, car safety, and why you shouldn't skip leg day.
sections.keyTakeaway: More mass or more acceleration = more force needed.

sections.title: Third Law: Action-Reaction
sections.content: For every action, there's an equal and opposite reaction. When you push against a wall, the wall pushes back just as hard (that's why you don't phase through it). Rockets work by pushing gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up. Every force has a twin going the other way.
sections.keyTakeaway: Forces always come in pairs. Push = get pushed.

lesson.summary: Newton's three laws explain how everything moves. Objects are lazy (inertia), force depends on mass and acceleration (F=ma), and forces always have partners (action-reaction).
